newsitem.title: UK: First results promising in 747 bomb-proof test.
newsitem.headline: First results promising in 747 bomb-proof test.

text.p: An experiment to blow up an old Jumbo jet may have brought the world a step closer to bomb-proof commercial aircraft, officials said on Monday.

In a spectacular trial, scientists from a research wing of Britain's defence ministry set off four explosive charges inside a pressurised obsolete Boeing 747-100 on Saturday to test two strengthened baggage containers and a section of reinforced hull.
The test, sponsored by Britain's Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) and the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), went according to plan, CAA spokesman Richard Wright said.
"All four charges were detonated, it appears...the two modified baggage containers and the blast-absorbent hold lining each provided a significant amount of protection," Wright said.
"We're very satisfied with the initial results."
Wright said it would be weeks before scientists from the Defence Evaluation and Research Agency (DERA), who carried out the test, would be able to submit a report.
"It's really too close to say how long international regulation will take, but the fact that the test appeared to have gone to plan will be a step along the road to any future regulation," he said.

The experiment was the culmination of a five-year, $5 million research program triggered by the death of 270 people in the bombing of a Pan Am Boeing 747 which crashed to earth in Lockerbie, Scotland in 1988.
The CAA said it was not so much the bomb that destroyed the Pan Am 747, but the wind pressure, temperature and altitude which ripped open the breach in the hull, causing "catastrophic damage".
The trial tested new methods of containing a bomb blast so as not to breach the aircraft skin.
Reporters were allowed to get within 100 metres (yards) of the destroyed 747 on Saturday to assess the damage.

The forward part of the giant plane, which held a hardened container designed by the FAA on the left side and a standard container next to a section of reinforced hull on the right side, looked unaffected by the blasts.
The aft section, which held a strengthened container designed by the CAA on the right-hand side behind the wing and a control charge with no added protection, was blown apart.
The left side of the plane behind the wing was blown wide open and the blast had all but split the aircraft in two. The tail section lay crumpled on the tarmac.
The effect of the undisclosed amount of explosive on the unprotected hull was as expected, Wright said.

The plane would remain where it was blown up, at the former U.S. Air Force Strategic Air Command base at Bruntingthorpe, about 100 miles (160 km) north of London, until a full examination and record of the debris had been made.
"There will be a very thorough investigation in situ before we move anything...so the plane will be there for a while," Wright said.
